frames.narration: A user edits a page. The request belongs to one workspace, and that workspace's ID is the partition key. Every block belongs to exactly one workspace, so everything this request needs lives in the same place.

The routing code, which lives in the application, turns the workspace ID into a uniform bucket, then into a physical database, and then into a logical shard, which is a Postgres schema such as schema001. There is no routing table to keep in step: this one rule is the single source of truth.
The write runs against that schema's own copy of the block table, on one database. Each database holds 15 logical schemas, and no query has to look at another database to answer for this workspace.

During the migration, before the switch, the same write also went to the old monolith, which was still the source of truth. The change was recorded in an audit log as well, because logical replication could not keep up with the write volume on the block table during the initial snapshot.

A catch-up script replays the audit log into the new databases, while a backfill copies the old data across. The backfill compares record versions and skips any record that already has a newer update, so old data never overwrites a fresh change. The final backfill ran for about three days.

Before anything depends on the new databases, they are checked. A script samples random UUIDs and compares adjacent ranges. 'Dark' reads fetch each record from both sides, compare them, throw the sharded copy away and log any difference. Users still see the monolith's answer. The post says dark reads made the API slower.

When the checks are clean, Notion switches over in a five-minute maintenance window. Reads and writes now go to the sharded databases. A reverse audit log and script were ready to carry changes back to the monolith if something had gone wrong. The post says they were not needed.
